course.name: Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences II

question.text: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $z=x^2+y^2$ that is subject to the constraint $x^2 + y^2 \leq 1.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

In this case, our surface is given by

\[ z = x^2+y^2, \qquad (x,y)\in D \]

where the region $D$ is given by

\[ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x^2+y^2\leq 1 \big\}, \]

as shown below.

Now, since

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2+y^2) = 2x, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(x^2+y^2) = 2y, \\[5pt] \end{align*}

the surface area is given by

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+(2x)^2+(2y)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+4x^2+4y^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+4(x^2+y^2)} \: \text{d}A. \end{align*}

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as \[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain \begin{align} \iint\limits_{D} \sqrt{1+4(x^2 + y^2)} \,\textrm d A & = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \sqrt{1+4r^2} \, r\,\textrm{d}r\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} r\sqrt{1+4r^2} \,\textrm{d}r\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_0^{2\pi} \, \textrm{d}\theta \int_{0}^{1} r\sqrt{1+4r^2} \, \textrm{d}r \\[5pt] & =2\pi \int_{0}^{1} r\sqrt{1+4r^2} \, \textrm{d}r. \end{align}

Setting $u=1+4r^2,$ we get $\text{d}u = 8r\, \text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

\[ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline r & 0 & 1 \\ \hline u & 1 & 5 \\ \hline \end{array} \]

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

\begin{align} 2\pi \int_{0}^{1} r\sqrt{1+4r^2} \, \textrm{d}r &= 2\pi \cdot\dfrac{1}{8} \int_{1}^{5} \sqrt u \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{4} \int_{1}^{5} u^{1/2} \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{4} \cdot \dfrac23\left[u^{3/2}\right]_{1}^5 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{6} \left[u^{3/2}\right]_{1}^5 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{6} \left[5^{3/2} - 1\right] \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\pi(5\sqrt{5} - 1)}{6} . \end{align}

question.text: Find the surface area of the part of the surface $z=xy$ that is subject to the constraint $x^2 + y^2 \leq 1.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

In this case, our surface is given by

\[ z =xy, \qquad (x,y)\in D \]

where the region $D$ is given by

\[ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: x^2+y^2\leq 1 \big\}, \]

as shown below.

Now, since

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(xy) = y, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(xy) =x, \\[5pt] \end{align*}

the surface area is given by

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+(y)^2+(x)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+x^2+y^2} \: \text{d}A. \end{align*}

In polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ the region $D$ can be expressed as \[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, we obtain \begin{align} \iint\limits_{D} \sqrt{1+(x^2 + y^2)} \,\textrm d A & = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \sqrt{1+r^2} \, r\,\textrm{d}r\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} r\sqrt{1+r^2} \,\textrm{d}r\,\textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_0^{2\pi} \, \textrm{d}\theta \int_{0}^{1} r\sqrt{1+r^2} \, \textrm{d}r \\[5pt] & =2\pi \int_{0}^{1} r\sqrt{1+r^2} \, \textrm{d}r. \end{align}

Setting $u=1+r^2,$ we get $\text{d}u = 2r\, \text{d}r.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

\[ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline r & 0 & 1 \\ \hline u & 1 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array} \]

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

\begin{align} 2\pi \int_{0}^{1} r\sqrt{1+r^2} \, \textrm{d}r &= 2\pi \cdot\dfrac{1}{2} \int_{1}^{2} \sqrt u \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \pi \int_{1}^{2} u^{1/2} \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \pi \cdot\left[ \dfrac23 \,u^{3/2}\right]_{1}^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \left[u^{3/2}\right]_{1}^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3} \left[2^{3/2} - 1\right] \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2\pi(2\sqrt{2} - 1)}{3} . \end{align}

question.text: Find the surface area of the portion of the surface $z = 3 \sin x+2\sqrt{2}y $ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\sin{2x}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

In this case, our surface is given by

\[ z = 3 \sin x+2\sqrt{2}y , \qquad (x,y)\in D \]

where the region $D$ is given by

\[ D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \: 0 \leq y \leq \sin{2x} \right\}, \]

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, since

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(3 \sin x+2\sqrt{2}y) = 3\cos x, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(3 \sin x+2\sqrt{2}y) = 2\sqrt{2}, \\[5pt] \end{align*}

the surface area is given by

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+(3\cos x)^2+(2\sqrt{2})^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+9\cos^2 x+8} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{9\left(1+\cos^2 x\right)} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D 3\sqrt{1+\cos^2 x} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= 3\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{1+\cos^2 x} \int_{0}^{\sin 2x} \: \text{d}y \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= 3\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sqrt{1+\cos^2 x} \cdot y \, \Big|_{0}^{\sin 2x} \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= 3\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin 2x \sqrt{1+\cos^2 x} \: \text{d}x. \end{align*}

Setting $u=1+\cos^2 x,$ we get $\text{d}u = -\sin 2x \, \text{d}x.$ Also, the limits must be changed as follows:

\[ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline x & 0 & \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ \hline u & 2 & 1 \\ \hline \end{array} \]

Substituting these into our integral, we obtain

\begin{align*} 3\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin 2x \sqrt{1+\cos^2 x} \: \text{d}x &=3\int_{2}^{1} \sqrt{u} (-\text{d}u) \\[5pt] &= 3\int_{1}^{2} \sqrt{u} \: \text{d}u \\[5pt] &= 2u^{3/2} \, \Big|_{1}^{2} \\[5pt] &= 2\left(2^{3/2} - 1\right) \\[5pt] &= 4\sqrt{2}-2. \end{align*}

question.text: Find the surface area of the portion of the surface $z = \dfrac{4\sqrt{x^3}}{3} $ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y=\sqrt{1+4x}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=2.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

In this case, our surface is given by

\[ z = \dfrac{4\sqrt{x^3}}{3} , \qquad (x,y)\in D \]

where the region $D$ is given by

\[ D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 2, \: 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt{1+4x} \right\}, \]

as shown in the diagram below.

Now, since

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( \dfrac{4\sqrt{x^3}}{3} \right) = 2\sqrt{x}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( \dfrac{4\sqrt{x^3}}{3} \right) = 0, \\[5pt] \end{align*}

the surface area is given by

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(2\sqrt{x}\right)^2+(0)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+4x} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{1+4x}} \sqrt{1+4x} \: \text{d}y \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \sqrt{1+4x}\cdot y \, \Big|_{0}^{\sqrt{1+4x}} \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \sqrt{1+4x} \cdot \sqrt{1+4x}\: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} (1+4x) \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left(x+2x^2\right) \, \Big|_{0}^{2} \\[5pt] &= (2+8) - 0 \\[5pt] &= 10. \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \iint\limits_{D} \fbox{$\phantom{AAAAAAAA}$} \: \text{d}A, \qquad D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: \fbox{$\phantom{AAAAAA}$}\, \big\} \]

The integral above gives the surface area of the part of the surface $x = y^3+e^z$ that lies inside the elliptical cylinder $\dfrac{y^2}4+\dfrac{z^2}9 = 1.$ From left to right, what are the missing expressions?
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $x=f(y,z)$ with $(y,z)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S = \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

In this case, our surface is given by

\[ x = y^3+e^z, \qquad \dfrac{y^2}4+\dfrac{z^2}9 \leq 1. \]

Now, since

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\big(y^3+e^z\big) = 3y^2, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial z} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial z}\big(y^3+e^z\big) = e^z, \\[5pt] \end{align*}

the surface area is

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \, \text{d}S &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial y}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \sqrt{1+\left(3y^2\right)^2+\big(e^z\big)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D {\color{blue}\sqrt{1+9y^4 +e^{2z}}} \: \text{d}A. \end{align*}

Therefore, the correct answer is

$\qquad$ $\sqrt{1+9y^4 +e^{2z}} \quad$ and $\quad \dfrac{y^2}4+\dfrac{z^2}9 \leq 1.$
